newsitem.title: GERMANY: German parties wheel out big guns for local vote.
newsitem.headline: German parties wheel out big guns for local vote.

text.p: Germany's political parties are wheeling out the big guns for local elections on Sunday which they see as this year's main test of voter reaction to record unemployment and wrangling over tax and pension reform.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl and leaders of all main parties have flocked to the state of Hesse to drum up support among 4.5 million eligible voters who will elect local councils including the city parliament for Frankfurt, Germany's financial capital.
While Kohl has described the vote as a signal for the outcome of the 1998 general election, pollsters say it will give a distorted picture of nationwide political sentiment.

The Hesse elections come at a difficult time for Kohl's centre-right coalition which according to a recent opinion poll would have lost its majority in the Bundestag or lower house of parliament if a general election had been held last weekend.
The main problem for Kohl is that he has presided over a steady rise in unemployment to 4.66 million people in January, a level last seen in the 1930s when Adolf Hitler came to power.

The jobless rise has alarmed the population, sparked heavy criticism of the government for its apparent inability to handle the crisis and looks set to jeopardize Kohl's pet project -- European monetary union.

At the same time speculation is growing that Germany's longest serving chancellor may be losing his ability to maintain strict discipline within his coalition parties which continue to squabble over pension and tax reform.

Despite politicians' claims that Hesse will reflect the judgement of voters on national issues, opinion polls suggest there is a clear divergence between how people will vote on Sunday and how they would vote in a general election.

"This is a local election which is extremely different from a national election," said Dieter Roth, a polling expert at the Electoral Research Group, regarded by politicians and pundits as one of the country's most reliable research firms.

Roth said voter turnout at local council elections tends to be far lower than in general elections -- about 65 percent compared with 80 percent, and in many municipalities citizens' pressure groups have far more support than mainstream parties.

Besides, local elections are often decided not by party allegiance but by the personality of candidates while the issues at stake -- local traffic problems, building projects or waste disposal -- are often far removed from national politics.
"This virtually precludes seeing this local election as a test of sentiment for the general election," Roth said.
"Politicians like to do this to be able to pick out something from the results to make themselves look good. And journalists like to follow them to find something sensational."

Recent polls show that despite Kohl's problems at the national level, his Christian Democrats (CDU) will gain in the election to Frankfurt's parliament on Sunday, mainly due to the popularity of its CDU mayor, Petra Roth.
The Social Democrats (SPD), in opposition in Bonn, are expected to emerge as clear losers, according to a poll by the Mannheim-based Ipos institute published last Sunday.
The poll puts CDU support at 37 percent, up from 33.4 percent in the last local election in 1993.
